chapter: Clarence Williams's 1936 article and the dispute
title: La Rocca's rebuttal: Williams's background and doubts about Buddy Bolden
summary: La Rocca attacks Williams's biography and says he never heard of Bolden, calling the Bolden stories pro-Negro propaganda by Stearns, Hammond and Dr. Sushan.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Buddy Bolden and Buddy Petit: the trumpet legends

blocks.x: Now, I just showed you the kind of propaganda that the people put out. They all knew about Tiger Rag. Now, here's a Negro. I'm going to give you his record. And if I'm wrong, then the world is wrong. This Negro lived in Plaquemine, Louisiana, at the age of about six to eight years old, worked as a shoeshine boy for Ferdinand Herbert, who operated a barbershop in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He came to New Orleans in his late teens. He lies as to hearing Buddy Bowling play. From the dates given in the second line of pro-Negro propaganda, Bowling was incarcerated in the crazy house in 1906. He or Bowling would never remember them. And I'm almost going on to 70 years old. And I never heard Bowling play. And Bowling was supposed to live on the eight blocks from me, back Jackson Avenue. And I never heard him. And if he was popular in music, I certainly would have known something about him, because I play most every night in the week. Now, these neighbors here, they go on fiction. And stories that has been told for a generation down. There's the big man. Supposed to say the same thing about my father. Oh, he's Italian. He couldn't play that. They couldn't play nothing. There ain't nobody. My daddy played music too. And he played a horn. I didn't say that you could hear him down in Memphis, Tennessee. Like they said that they heard Bowling down in Memphis, Tennessee. Where Handy took down his notes when he played. All this is fabulous lies. Created by a bunch of pro-communists, pro-Negro intelligents who are trying to give the Negro culture. Now, they have did plenty damage. Yet, if I went to court, it would take me all the money I got to prove that they did damage, in a way, a monetary damage to me. In other words, it could tell my royalties anything. They have never did that. They have tried to discredit me in many things because when they look at Tiger Ride, that's the essence of American music as played today. And they ought to discredit that. You have men like Marshall Stein, John Hammond, Dr. Sushaw, who's supposed to know about this music. Let me read you Dr. Sushaw's letter, or have it read into this thing here, in 1949. Would you read this letter of Dr. Sushaw's in there?
